newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela awaits Zaire's Kabila, Mobutu goes home.
newsitem.headline: Mandela awaits Zaire's Kabila, Mobutu goes home.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela, unbowed by his failure to broker Zairean peace talks in Congo, on Thursday scheduled talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila on a South African proposal to avert a bloody civil war showdown.
Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela sent a plane to the Angolan enclave of Cabinda on Thursday to bring Kabila to Cape Town for an afternoon meeting.

He said South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki would remain in Pointe Noire, Congo, where the talks were to have taken place on Wednesday, to maintain contact with President Mobutu Sese Seko's government delegation.
"In our view the talks are not derailed. Kabila has not said that he will not talk, he has merely raised concerns about his security.
"We think there is still a very large opening for them both to walk through to achieve peace in Zaire," Mankahlana said.
South African government spokesman Ricky Naidoo said Mobutu left Pointe Noire on Thursday morning to return to the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
Members of his delegation, headed by Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda, boarded the South African navy icebreaker Outeniqua, which was to have hosted the talks, to see Mbeki.
Mobutu and Mandela arrived for the proposed shipboard meeting on Wednesday but Kabila, citing security concerns, refused to fly from Cabinda to the ship unless it sailed into international waters.
Asked whether Mandela, who refused to take the ship out to sea, was irritated by Kabila's behaviour, Mankahlana said:
"The president was very calm. The humanitarian tragedy unfolding in Zaire is unprecedented. There is no amount of patience he cannot find. He is compelled to continue."
Mankahlana said Mandela, Mbeki and United Nations envoy Mohamed Sahnoun spent an hour with Mobutu late on Wednesday, discussing the talks breakdown and the way forward.
He said they discussed a two-page South African proposal for a transition to democracy in Zaire after more than 30 years of autocratic rule by Mobutu.
Mankahlana said the plan had the support of most African and Western governments, although France had raised some concerns.
He said Mobutu delivered a lengthy response written in French, but said it did not undermine the peace process: "They have raised pertinent questions which are not insurmountable."
South African government spokesman Pieter Swanepoel said the proposal called for a legal transitional structure to replace the present constitutional government.
"It's very important because if we don't get a long-term political solution the matter is going to be resolved militarily and that's no long-term solution for the situation in Zaire," he said.

A member of the Organisation of African Unity delegation in Pointe Noire told reporters the OAU was very pessimistic about prospects for a negotiated peace following the cancellation of the second face-to-face meeting between Mobutu and Kabila.
Mobutu agreed at talks on the same ship on May 4 to hand power to an elected president, but no arrangements were agreed.
Kabila, both then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.

Sahnoun said on Wednesday he and Mandela, who has headed the African peace initiative, had not abandoned hope. "We are not going to give up. We will continue to try to avoid another humanitarian tragedy," he said.
Rebel spokesmen said Kabila, 56, whose forces now control three-quarters of Africa's third largest nation, had insisted on talks at sea on security grounds.
Mobutu's government in Kinshasa said it remained ready to give peace talks a chance.
"We do not think that the dialogue has broken down," government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba said.
The capital, largely shut down on Wednesday by an opposition stay-home protest against Mobutu, spent its second night under curfew in the seven-month-old war. Troops have orders to shoot looters.
Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, have made lightning advances across the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.
Rebel radio suggested Kabila's forces were nearing the approaches to Kinshasa. The government dismissed such reports.
